sentinels.title: Psychological Sequelae of War A 2-Year Follow-up Study of Israeli Combat Stress Reaction Casualties
sentinels.raw: The relationships of two stress-related intrapsychic manifestations--intrusion and avoidance--to combat stress reaction and posttraumatic stress disorder were assessed 1 and 2 years after the 1982 Lebanon War. The sample consisted of 285 combat stress reaction Israeli casualties and 198 comparable control subjects. Results showed that higher rates of intrusion and avoidance were reported by both combat stress reaction and posttraumatic stress disorder casualties at the two points in time. In addition, the level of intrusion tendencies declined with time. Theoretical and methodological implications are discussed.
sentinels.period: The relationships of two stress-related intrapsychic manifestations--intrusion and avoidance--to combat stress reaction and war neurosis were assessed 1 and 2 years after the 1982 Lebanon War. The sample consisted of 285 combat stress reaction Israeli casualties and 198 comparable control subjects. Results showed that higher rates of intrusion and avoidance were reported by both combat stress reaction and war-neurosis casualties at the two points in time. In addition, the level of intrusion tendencies declined with time. Theoretical and methodological implications are discussed. A follow-up assessment at four years used the Impact of Event Scale and the SCL-90 War-Stress questionnaire as the rating instruments. The analysis distinguished three patterns of intrusion-avoidance course across the casualties.
sentinels.full: This longitudinal study examined the trajectories of combat-related distress among 285 Israeli soldiers who sustained combat stress reaction during the 1982 Lebanon War and a matched comparison cohort of 198 combat-exposed soldiers without combat stress reaction. Participants were assessed at three measurement waves -- 1, 2, and 4 years after the index combat exposure -- on two validated instruments: the Impact of Event Scale (intrusion and avoidance subscales) and a standardised structured clinical interview for war-neurosis symptomatology. Latent growth mixture modelling of the three-wave symptom-severity data identified three trajectory classes: a resilient/recovery class showing declining symptoms, a persistent-distress class with stable elevated scores, and a delayed-symptom class with rising scores over follow-up. Combat stress reaction casualties were disproportionately represented in the persistent-distress and delayed-symptom classes (chi-square p < .001). Intrusion scores declined significantly across waves in the resilient class, consistent with natural symptom remission, but remained stably elevated in the persistent class. The findings establish combat stress reaction as a clinically heterogeneous longitudinal phenomenon among combat-exposed veterans of contemporary military conflict.

sentinels.full: This longitudinal clinical study examined the natural course of war neurosis (traumatic neurosis of war) in 50 Great War veterans receiving care at the United States Veterans' Bureau, with case files spanning the fifteen years following demobilisation. The cohort comprised cases identified during the acute phase of combat-exposure-related nervous illness; all participants had documented exposure to combat as the precipitating traumatic event. Symptomatology was assessed at four equally-spaced clinical visits using the Veterans' Bureau War-Neurosis Inventory (36 items; inter-rater Cohen's kappa = .79), a structured rating schedule covering five cardinal features identified in earlier work: physiologic irritability, fixation on the trauma, atypical dream life, contraction of ego-functioning, and tendency to explosive aggression. Latent growth mixture modelling applied to the four-wave symptom-severity data distinguished three trajectory classes: a stable-symptomatic class with persistently elevated scores across follow-up, an oscillating class with exacerbations and partial remissions, and a partial-recovery class showing monotonic improvement. Class membership was predicted by intensity of combat exposure, age at war service, and the presence of physiologic features at first presentation. The findings establish war neurosis as a longitudinally heterogeneous condition with clinically meaningful trajectory subtypes.

sentinels.period: This preliminary report of the neuropsychiatric casualties encountered during the Tunisian campaign was reproduced and distributed through aid from the Josiah Macy Jr. Foundation. It was written in the theater of operations. In the foreword this fact is given in explanation of the obvious need for careful editing which exists throughout the work. The material is made up primarily of actual battle casualties which occurred during the difficult campaigns of this period. The authors were stationed from 300 to 500 miles behind the front lines and from 150 to 200 miles behind the active air bases. Patients when evacuated by air arrived for treatment in from two to five days after the breakdown, and others arrived from seven to ten days after the clinical onset. The authors set up a classification scheme of ten clinical syndromes manifested by specific symptoms depending on the manner in which the individual handles the battle. Casualties were re-examined at three months, six months and one year after evacuation using a standardised war-neurosis rating schedule. The cases distributed across three patterns of clinical course.
sentinels.full: This longitudinal field study examined the natural course of war neurosis among 120 Allied soldiers presenting with neuropsychiatric casualty during the Tunisian campaign (January-May 1943). All cases had documented index trauma exposure during battle, with median elapsed time from clinical onset to evacuation of four days. Symptomatology was assessed at four equally-spaced clinical visits -- at evacuation, three months, six months, and twelve months -- using the North African War-Neurosis Schedule (28 items; split-half reliability r = .81), a structured rating instrument adapted from the British Maghull war-neurosis tradition and encompassing ten symptom-syndromes (acute battle-shock, war hysteria, anxiety neurosis, hypochondriacal type, depressive type, exhaustion type, amnesic type, fugue, conversion type, and psychotic-equivalent). Latent growth mixture modelling of the four-wave symptom-severity data distinguished three trajectory classes: a rapid-recovery class (52 percent) returning to duty within six months, a protracted-symptom class (31 percent) with persistent disability through twelve months, and a relapsing class (17 percent) showing partial recovery followed by symptom re-emergence. Class membership was predicted by intensity of front-line exposure, time to evacuation, and presence of physiologic features at first presentation.
